name: Mathspace
line: Mathspace works in assigned tasks and separate tests. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review happen at every problem.
description: AMP vs Mathspace: Mathspace works in assigned tasks and separate check-ins. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous, at every problem.
verdict: Mathspace is built around tasks a teacher assigns, with a separate adaptive test, the Skills Check-in, and each line of working checked as it is entered [2][1][8]. In AMP, assessment and teaching are continuous. Every answer updates the learner's level and sets the next problem, and each problem carries its own hint, lesson and worked answer.

reasons.title: Continuous assessment
reasons.body: AMP has no separate test. Every answer updates the learner's level in that part of math and sets the next problem: new work within reach, a gap to close, or an old skill due back. Mathspace measures in Skills Check-ins, a separate adaptive test reported as a grade level, and recommends tasks from the results [1][5].

reasons.title: The problem is the unit
reasons.body: In AMP, everything hangs off the problem: a hint that gives the first step, a lesson with a worked example, a video lesson, the worked answer afterward, and links to the skills it builds on and leads to. In Mathspace the unit is the task. A teacher assigns it with a due date [2]. An adaptive task runs in rounds and ends after a set amount of practice, not when the student reaches mastery [3].

reasons.title: Learned means right without help
reasons.body: In AMP an answer given after a hint or a lesson is marked as helped and does not count as learned. A skill counts when the learner gets it right without help, more than once. In a Mathspace adaptive task, a correct final answer earns diamonds even if the student used hints, videos or the lesson. Only the Next Step button withholds them [4].

reasons.title: Moving on, and going back
reasons.body: In AMP repeated misses send practice back to what the skill builds on. Mathspace lists a topic's missing prerequisite skills as gaps, and recommends a topic as ready only once its prerequisites are mastered [6][5]. Its readiness article leaves the choice to the student and suggests teachers set a date for filling gaps [6].

reasons.title: Continuous review
reasons.body: In AMP, learned skills come back in ordinary practice, at growing intervals, mixed with other math. Mathspace's Revision bank holds questions a student has not yet answered correctly. A missed question returns after some time, with no interval given, and one correct answer removes it for good [7]. We found no scheduled review of skills already mastered [7]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% on the researchers' own test a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [27].

reasons.title: A level for each part of math
reasons.body: AMP keeps a separate level for each part of math, from counting through precalculus. A learner further along in one part than another gets work at both levels. In Mathspace a student's grade level comes from their class unless a teacher overrides it, and recommended tasks run from grade 3 up to that grade [13].

rows.range: Content mapped to US standards for grades 3 to 12 [12].
rows.start: A separate adaptive test, the Skills Check-in, reported as a grade level such as 8.5 [1].
rows.teaching: Textbook lessons with videos, hints for the current step, worked solutions, and Milo, an AI chat tutor, beside the work [18][10][20][19].
rows.next: Tasks a teacher assigns, and recommended tasks the student picks among. Inside a task, questions get harder as the student shows understanding [2][5].
rows.mastery: For an adaptive task, a target of Proficient or Mastered, set by the teacher. Tasks end after a set amount of practice. Answers after hints still earn diamonds [2][3][4].
rows.review: Revision: missed questions return after a while and leave after one correct answer. No scheduled review of mastered skills found [7].
rows.print: Printable worksheets for select textbooks, and worksheets a teacher builds for a class in beta, with answer keys [14][15].
rows.adult: A teacher builds and assigns tasks with due dates, sets the target mastery, and reads reports [2][16].
rows.reports: Task, student and class reports with each student's work on each question, a live view, and an administrator dashboard [16].
rows.evidence: One Utah state evaluation comparing users with non-users: positive only for students using it over 33 minutes a week [21]. Evidence for ESSA: no rating [24].

theirs: Mathspace is made by Mathspace Pty Ltd of Sydney, Australia [17]. It is an online math program: an interactive textbook, practice that checks each line of working, adaptive tasks, diagnostic check-ins and an AI chat tutor called Milo [18][19]. US content is mapped to standards for grades 3 to 12 [12].

Work comes from tasks a teacher assigns, practice recommended after check-ins, and a Revision bank of missed questions [2][5][7]. Inside a question, the student writes the solution line by line, and each line is marked as it is entered [8]. Hints, for some questions a video, the lesson and a Next Step button sit beside the work [10]. After a task, Fix mode lets the student redo missed questions until the due date [11].
credit: It checks each line of a student's working as it is entered, and accepts valid methods its authors did not foresee [8][9].
Hints are written for the step the student is on [10].
Every textbook question has a full worked solution, with a similar problem to try [20].

theirs: The outcome evidence we found is one state evaluation. The Utah Education Policy Center at the University of Utah studied the 2018-19 school year of the Utah STEM Action Center's grant program [21]. It compared 2,105 Mathspace users with 11,319 students from matched schools that did not use the funded programs, adjusting for student characteristics. It was not a randomized trial [21].

Results depended on use. Only students using Mathspace more than 33 minutes a week differed significantly: a 9% higher probability of proficiency on Utah's RISE test and growth percentiles 3.92 points higher. The two middle usage groups showed no significant difference, and students using it under 6 minutes a week had growth percentiles 4.67 points lower. Half the users logged 12 minutes a week or less [21]. Students who use a program most can differ from the rest before they start, so the study cannot show that Mathspace caused the gain.

Mathspace's Parents page cites a study of 94,000 students and a 53% increase in the likelihood of proficiency [22]. The company's blog places that study in Utah's 2017-18 school year, says 6,588 of those students used Mathspace, and gives no design or effect sizes [23]. Evidence for ESSA lists Mathspace without a rating: "No studies met inclusion requirements" [24]. We found no What Works Clearinghouse intervention report for it when we checked [25]. EdReports reviewed its high school series for alignment and usability, not learning outcomes [26].
ours: The two findings that bear most on this comparison: a review of ten common study techniques rated practice testing and spaced practice as high utility [28], and in a randomized trial that meets What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% on the researchers' own test a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [27]. AMP applies both at every problem.

AMP's own outcome studies are planned: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. The research behind each part of AMP is in our report, and AMP is open source.

them: You want each line of a student's written working checked as it is entered [8].
amp: You want assessment, teaching and review in the same practice, with no separate tests.
You want a skill to count only when it is right without help.
You want learned skills to keep coming back in practice.
Your learner is at different levels in different parts of math, or you want one program from counting through precalculus.
You want printed workbooks made from your child's own record, with worked answer keys.

questions.question: How is AMP different from Mathspace?
questions.answer: Mathspace works in tasks a teacher assigns, with a separate Skills Check-in, and checks each line of working [2][1][8]. AMP has no separate test: every answer sets the next problem, each problem carries its own teaching, and learned skills return in ordinary practice.

questions.question: Does Mathspace work?
questions.answer: The one outcome study we found, a Utah state evaluation, compared users with non-users. Only students using Mathspace more than 33 minutes a week did significantly better, and the study cannot show cause [21]. Evidence for ESSA lists it without a rating [24].

questions.question: Can a learner use both?
questions.answer: Yes. They are separate programs. AMP places a learner from their first answers, whatever else they use.
